# Emitted Runtime Bodies

## Documentation

A compiled program CONTAINS more code than its author declares. The entry stub `mrt_start`, the
`__mm_*`/`__slab_*` allocator, the `__str_*`/`__managed_*` families and the `__destruct_*`
thunks are all synthesized by the backend, and a `TargetIr` pin shows NONE of them: the
rendering holds only the functions parsed from the PROGRAM's own source, because the shared
scaffolding is identical in every test and would be pure noise in all of them.

The **library** is withheld by the same rule and for the same reason. The compiler compiles `stdlib/`
from source into the same module as the program, so `String.trim`, `Array.reserve` and every
grapheme helper the cone reaches are ordinary module functions the printer could render. Rendered,
they would outweigh the program in every pin — and what that noise costs is not disk: an edit
anywhere in `stdlib/` would move every pin at once, burying the signal the pins exist to carry.

That default is right for the scaffolding and wrong for a body that is itself under test.
`__str_bytes_view` publishes a zero-copy `Array with Byte` over a String's own bytes and
counts a reference on the allocation those bytes live in; getting that count wrong is a
use-after-free that BALANCES — the matching release disappears with it — so neither the
exit code, nor the leak gate, nor a pin of the program's own functions can see it.

### Naming a body to render: ```RequiredRuntime

A test opts one or more withheld functions INTO its own `TargetIr` pin with a
`RequiredRuntime` block, one name per line:

```
__str_bytes_view
```

A **stdlib** body is named the same way and by the same list — `String.trim`, `Array.reserve` —
which is how a case whose subject IS a library body pins the one body it is about. The name has to
be one the program REACHES: an unreached stdlib function is eliminated before the back end, so
naming it renders nothing and is refused exactly as a misspelling is.

Only the named functions are added, and only to that test's rendering; every test without
the block renders only the program's own functions. A name
that matches no emitted function — or one that names a function the rendering already
shows — is refused by the compiler, so a misspelling cannot silently pin nothing. An
EMPTY block is refused by the spec parser for the same reason: it would render no body at
all, leaving the pin identical to a test that never asked.

### What it pins, and what it does not

⚠ **This block pins the compiler's Target IR — what the backend DECIDED — not the bytes the
linker wrote.** It is the `printDataSection` half of the pair, not the ```RequiredData
half: the text is the printer's own rendering of a lowered, register-allocated body, so it
moves on any change to lowering, allocation or block structure, and is BLIND to anything
below it. An instruction encoder that emits different bytes for the same mnemonic and
operands leaves this pin identical. ```RequiredData / ```RequiredRdata are the gates
that read the linked image back; ```RequiredRuntime is not one of them.

### A hand-assembled chunk: the same block, rendered as BYTES

Some of what the compiler emits is not IR at all. The panic runtime (`mrt_panic` and its
backtrace walker), the green-thread pieces (`__gt_context_switch`, `__gt_trampoline`,
`__gt_morestack`) and arm64's entry stub are assembled as raw machine bytes, so they never
enter the module's function list and there is no body to print for them.

They are still named, and the same ```RequiredRuntime block reaches them: a name no IR
function answers is offered to the emitted chunks, and the one bearing it renders a hex dump
instead of a body.

```
chunk @mrt_panic {
    0000: 55 48 89 e5 …
}
```

⚠ **The bytes are the chunk's own, BEFORE linking** — every intra-module call still shows a
zero displacement (`e8 00 00 00 00`) and every imported call a zero IAT slot. That is
deliberate and it is what makes the pin usable: the linked image resolves those against
where everything landed, so a dump cut from it would move whenever anything ELSE in the
program changed size. A chunk's own buffer depends on nothing outside the chunk — the same
reason a printed IR body shows a branch LABEL rather than a displacement. What this pin
holds is therefore the ASSEMBLER's output, exactly as the IR form pins the lowering's.

## Tests

<!-- test: string-bytes-view-body -->
The byte-view runtime entry, reached through `stdlib/FilePath.maxon`'s own cone.
`__str_bytes_view`'s `bvcoown` block carries the incref that keeps the receiver alive for as long
as the buffer value exists; `bvret` is the arm an IMMORTAL record takes, which increfs nothing
because a `.rdata` record can neither be freed nor written.

⚠ **THE BODY ALLOCATES NOTHING.** A String record embeds the buffer record whole and keeps its flag
at `@48`, so `return managed` is served by handing back the receiver: one capacity test and one
`__mm_incref`. This case's `TargetIr` pin is where that shows as instructions rather than as a trace.

⚠ **THIS CASE NAMES ONE BODY.** `String.byteAtOrPanic` is `stdlib/String.maxon:299`, whose own body is
`try byteAt(index) otherwise panic(…)` — ordinary Maxon, compiled as an ordinary function, with no
runtime chunk to render. `String.addressableBytes()`'s corpus body is `return managed`, and reading a
fused wrapper's inline `managed` is exactly what mints this entry (`Parser.emitFieldLoad`).

```maxon
function main() returns ExitCode
	let p = FilePath from "a/b.txt"
	if p.fileExtension() == ".txt" 'ok'
		return 0
	end 'ok'
	return 1
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
0
```
```RequiredRuntime
__str_bytes_view
```

func @__str_bytes_view {
  entry:
    x64.pushReg rbp
    x64.movRegReg rbp, rsp
    x64.pushReg rbx
    x64.prologue 40
    x64.movRegReg rbx, rcx
    x64.loadRegBaseDisp.word64 rax, [rbx + 16]
    x64.cmpRegImm32 rax, -4
    x64.jcc equal, bvret
  bvcoown:
    x64.movRegReg rcx, rbx
    x64.callDirect __mm_incref
  bvret:
    x64.movRegReg r8, rbx
    x64.epilogue 40
    x64.popReg rbx
    x64.popReg rbp
    x64.ret
}

<!-- test: allocator-shape-is-one-in-a-program-with-no-scheduler -->
**THE ALLOCATOR HAS ONE SHAPE, AND A PROGRAM WITH NO SCHEDULER CARRIES ALL OF IT.** This program builds
one array, pushes one element and returns; it spawns nothing and reads no counter. The four bodies
rendered here are what every heap program carries: `__slab_alloc` and `__slab_free` read the scheduler
word out of the slab's state head and take the raw row as its sole writer when it is 0, step that row's
raw traffic columns with a plain add, and probe the cached span's owner; `__mm_alloc` and `__mm_free`
step the tracked columns the same way. The serialised arm — the TLS read, the atomic steps and the lock —
is rendered beside them, reached only once `__sched_init_procs` has published the word. A pin that
lost the scheduler-word probe, the owner probe or a column step would be a compiler that had grown a
second shape for programs without a scheduler.
```maxon
typealias Byte = int(0 to u8.max)
typealias ByteArray = Array with Byte

function main() returns ExitCode
	var buf = ByteArray.create()
	buf.push(1)
	return buf.count() as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: error-ordinal-in-an-emitted-body -->
An emitted body transcribes an error enum's ORDINAL as a literal — `__managed_set`'s `rejcont` block
returns ordinal 0 with the error flag set, which is the wire format an `otherwise` arm decodes. The
ordinal is a positional fact about a case LIST, and nothing else in the suite can see the literal
the runtime actually carries: the run only sees that *some* error came back.

```maxon
function main() returns ExitCode
	var names = ["a", "b"]
	try names.set(1, value: "c") otherwise panic("set rejected a valid index")
	return 0
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
0
```
```RequiredRuntime
__managed_set
```

<!-- test: entry-stub-body -->
The `mrt_` band, from the other side of `isRuntimeFunction`'s two prefixes: the entry
stub every program has and no other case's `TargetIr` pin shows.

⭐⭐ **THE FIRST THING IT DOES IS INSTALL THE FAULT HANDLER** — `mrt_runtime_init`, ahead of any user code,
so a division that traps before `main` has run still reaches a diagnostic. The stub touches the CONSOLE not
at all: encoding is decided per WRITE, inside `mrt_write_stream`, which asks each standard stream whether
its handle is a console and converts to UTF-16 for the ones that are. Nothing process-wide is set, so a
program that never writes to a console changes nothing about the one it was launched from.

⚠ **THE STUB IS PINNED HERE BECAUSE NOTHING ELSE IN THE SUITE RENDERS IT** — every `TargetIr` pin withholds
the emitted runtime unless its case names it, and this case is the one that does.

⛔⛔ **AND THE CONSOLE ROAD ITSELF IS PINNED BY NOTHING, HERE OR ANYWHERE.** Every case's output is CAPTURED
— a pipe, never a console — so every suite run takes the NOT-A-CONSOLE road from end to end, and a case
could not ask which road it took in any event: a program cannot see which API carried its own writes. Which
MECHANISM an image was built with is answerable from the image's bytes and is gated in
`tests/console-write/`; whether the conversion is CORRECT is covered by hand against a real console, and by
nothing automated. Do not read a green suite as evidence about it.

sequence; arm64 emits its own, so the pin is meaningless there rather than merely different.
The panic runtime is HAND-ASSEMBLED bytes, not `TargetOp`s — so it has no IR body, is skipped
by every rendering that does not name it, and has no other gate of any kind: not an exit code (a program
that never panics never enters it), not the leak gate, not a section pin, not a body pin. It is
installed in EVERY x64 program, so the smallest possible one pins it. The zero
displacements are the unresolved call fixups the linker fills in; see the note above.

```maxon
function deepRecurse(n Integer) returns Integer
	Scheduler.yield()
	if n == 0 'base'
		return 0
	end 'base'
	return deepRecurse(n - 1) + 1
end 'deepRecurse'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let p = async deepRecurse(200)
	let r = await p
	return r as ExitCode
end 'main'
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

<!-- test: linux-lock-enter-makes-no-kernel-call-uncontended -->
<!-- unsupported-targets: x64-windows, arm64-macos -->
**THE UNCONTENDED RUNTIME-LOCK ENTER MAKES NO KERNEL CALL.** A runtime lock is a zero-initialised word,
and its uncontended enter is one byte exchange on that word, inline in the body that takes the lock
(`a-runtime-lock-enter-is-an-atomic-on-its-word-with-no-call` pins it). Only an enter whose exchange
displaced a nonzero byte reaches `__rtlock_enter_slow`, and only an outermost leave whose exchange
displaced a byte other than the bare held bit reaches `__rtlock_release`; both take the displaced byte as
their second argument. Those two bodies are what this pin renders. A NESTED enter also displaces a nonzero
byte, because the word is held, and `__rtlock_enter_slow` answers it first: the owner slot holds the
caller's own thread token, so it steps the hold's depth, puts back the sleeper hint the exchange cleared,
and returns before any other call.

⭐ **A CONTENDED ENTER SPINS BEFORE IT SLEEPS, AND SLEEPS ON ITS MACHINE'S OWN EVENT, AS GO'S `lock2`
DOES.** A runtime lock is held for a few instructions, so a thread that finds it held is likelier to see it
freed by spinning than by a futex round trip, which costs the waiter a sleep and the releaser a wake. The
contended path retries the acquire between a bounded active spin (`mrt_host_spin_pause`: `pause` on x64,
an `isb` and a counter-timed delay on arm64) and a bounded passive spin (`mrt_host_thread_yield`: `sched_yield`), and only then
pushes its machine onto the sleeper list in the lock word and waits on that machine's own event (Go's
`m.waitsema`) — a futex wait, `mrt_host_wait_one` with an infinite timeout on both Linux lanes.
A machine's first sleep creates that event (`mrt_host_wait_new`); a thread with no machine yet only
yields. A leave that pops a sleeper sets that machine's event, which issues a futex wake only when the
sleeper had announced itself on the event (`mrt_host_event_set`). Every spin is bounded, so a holder that does not release soon still costs the waiter one sleep rather than a
core.

Neither body issues a kernel call itself: no `syscall` on x64, no `svc` on arm64. Each reaches the kernel
only through those host chunks, and every such call sits behind a displaced byte or a sleeper found
in the word; the only other call is `__rt_abort`, on a misused lock or a refused event. A kernel call
anywhere else in these bodies is a cost every contended round trip pays before it has had a chance to
spin.

The program spawns a service, so the scheduler is installed and its locks take their multi-thread form;
a program that never starts a second thread links a contended path that aborts instead of waiting.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
__rtlock_enter_slow
__rtlock_release
```

<!-- test: a-lock-spin-pause-waits-a-time-on-arm64-as-go-s-procyield-does -->
**A RUNTIME LOCK'S ACTIVE SPIN IS GO's `procyield(30)`, AND ON ARM64 THAT IS THIRTY NANOSECONDS BY THE
COUNTER, NOT THIRTY HINTS.** A contended enter spins before it sleeps (`mutexActiveSpinSize` is 30 in
`lock_spinbit.go`). On x86 the argument counts `PAUSE` instructions, so `mrt_host_spin_pause` is a loop of
`pause`. On arm64 Go's `procyieldAsm` counts NANOSECONDS: an `ISB`, then a delay read off the virtual
counter `CNTVCT_EL0` scaled by the counter frequency `CNTFRQ_EL0`, with the first 18 ns charged to the
opening `ISB`. A `YIELD` loop is a hint some cores execute as nothing (thirty of them take 2.3 ns on Apple
silicon), so a wait counted in hints is not a wait; the counter ticks at a fixed rate on every core.

What the arm64 pins show is that chunk: a zero count returns at once, the opening `isb`, a count of 18 or
fewer returns, the count less 18 is scaled to counter ticks as `(n + n/16) * CNTFRQ_EL0 >> 30`, and the delay
loop is an `isb`, a `CNTVCT_EL0` read and an unsigned compare of the elapsed ticks against the delay. A
`yield` anywhere in it is the loop this case exists to keep out. The x64 pins show a `test` that returns at
once on a zero count, then the `pause` loop, which is Go's `procyieldAsm` on amd64.
```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
mrt_host_spin_pause
```

<!-- test: arm64-atomics-are-lse-on-macos-and-hwcap-checked-on-linux -->
<!-- unsupported-targets: x64-windows, x64-linux -->
**EVERY ARM64 ATOMIC IS AN LSE INSTRUCTION ON MACOS, AND ON LINUX IS ONE BEHIND THE KERNEL's HWCAP BIT, AS GO's
ARE.** Go's `internal/runtime/atomic` on arm64 emits `CASALD`, `SWPALB` and `LDADDALD` when
`cpu.ARM64.HasATOMICS` is set and an `LDAXR`/`STLXR` loop otherwise, and darwin always has them. This
compiler does the same for every atomic it emits, the lock's byte exchange included: on arm64-macos the
instruction is the LSE one alone, and on arm64-linux it follows a test of the byte `mrt_linux_hwcap_probe`
set from `AT_HWCAP`'s `HWCAP_ATOMICS` bit (bit 8) before any thread exists, with the reservation loop as the
fallback.

`__gt_preempt_m` is the witness because it is a hand-assembled body that claims a machine's
`signalPending` word with a compare-and-swap, so its bytes show the encoding. On macos they hold `casal`
and no `ldaxr`. On linux they hold the flag load (an `adrp`/`add` pair and a `ldrb`), a `cbz` over the `casal`,
and the `ldaxr`/`stlxr` loop after it.
```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

<!-- test: a-linux-event-set-wakes-only-a-sleeper-that-announced-itself -->
<!-- unsupported-targets: x64-windows, arm64-macos -->
**A LINUX `SetEvent` ISSUES `FUTEX_WAKE` ONLY WHEN A WAITER HAS ANNOUNCED ITSELF, AS GO's `semawakeup` DOES.**
Go's futex `semasleep` decrements the M's `waitsema` count before it sleeps and `semawakeup` increments it,
waking only when the count says a sleeper exists. A runtime lock's sleeper sleeps on its machine's event, and
a wake that arrives before the sleep, or after a spin took the lock, found nobody to wake and still paid the
system call. The event's signal word is the same announcement: 0 nobody waiting and not signalled, 1
signalled, 2 a waiter announced and is asleep or about to be. `mrt_host_event_set` exchanges the word's low
byte for 1 and issues `FUTEX_WAKE` only when the word it displaced was 2; a waiter publishes 2 with a
compare-and-swap from 0 before it enters `FUTEX_WAIT`, and the kernel's own check of the word against 2 closes
the window between the two.

What the pins show is `mrt_host_event_set`: a byte exchange, a compare of the displaced byte against 2, and
the `futex` call behind the branch that finds 2. A `futex` call that no comparison guards is the wake this
case exists to keep out. Windows's `SetEvent` and darwin's condition-variable signal are what Go's
`os_windows` and `os_darwin` `semawakeup` do, so those lanes have no subject here.
```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
mrt_host_event_set
```

```

<!-- test: a-library-body-named-into-the-golden -->
The LIBRARY half of the same block. `String.trim` is `stdlib/String.maxon`'s own code — withheld
from every rendering by default, exactly as `mrt_start` is — and this is the route that puts one
body back. The case is this door's only gate: withdraw the stdlib half of
`TargetPrinter.isSuppliedFunction` and the block stops pinning anything new (the rendering would
show `String.trim` anyway, and the compiler refuses a name it already shows); withdraw the
NAMING half and the compiler refuses the block outright. Either way this case goes red, which is
what a case that would otherwise only assert an exit code cannot do.

⚠ Its zero-argument sibling `String.trim#` — the overload that supplies
`CharacterSet.whitespacesAndNewlines()` — is what `main` actually calls, and it is NOT named here:
one body per name, and the pin shows the two-argument scan this pins rather than the forwarder.

```maxon
function main() returns ExitCode
	let s = "  abc  "
	return s.trim().byteLength() as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
3
```
```RequiredRuntime
String.trim
```

<!-- test: string-byte-at-body -->
`__managed_byte_at` — the THROWING, bounds-checked byte read behind `String.byteAt`. It leaves through the
dual-register `errorReturn` ABI carrying `__ManagedMemoryError.invalidByteRange`, which is exactly what
`stdlib/String.maxon:285` declares. The corpus's `hashString` is what installs it here, and this block is
its only gate.

⚠ **THE READ IS THE BUFFER'S.** `String.byteAt` is a corpus declaration whose own
`try managed.byteAt(index)` is the real call, so the read happens where the BUFFER's `byteAt`
happens — one entry point with one bound, rather than two graphs to keep in step. The
`RequiredRuntime` guard keeps the case from quietly pinning nothing: a name no program emits is a
loud panic (`TargetPrinter.requireEveryNameRendered`), which is the whole reason that guard exists.

```maxon
function main() returns ExitCode
	return hashString("a") mod 7
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
3
```
```RequiredRuntime
__managed_byte_at
```

<!-- test: a-mailbox-send-steps-its-lock-depth-with-a-plain-add -->
**THE LOCK DEPTH HAS ONE WRITER, SO ITS STEP IS A PLAIN READ-MODIFY-WRITE.** Every runtime lock enter
steps the calling machine's `MOffLocks` word up before the acquire, and every leave steps it down after the
release, so an asynchronous stop can refuse a thread that holds a runtime lock. The word belongs to ONE
machine, and only the OS thread running that machine writes it. Its readers are that same thread's own
signal handler (Linux and macOS), which program order already serves, and on x64-windows the monitor,
which reads it only while the thread is suspended. Neither needs the step to be atomic, so a locked
read-modify-write buys nothing and costs a full barrier at every enter and every leave: on x64 it is
`add qword [depth], ±1` with no `lock` prefix, and on arm64 a load, an add and a store.

`__mbox_send` is the witness because it is the smallest body that takes a runtime lock on every message:
one enter and one leave of its mailbox's lock on its append road and on its handoff road, and one leave on
each of its two refusing roads (a closed mailbox answers `stopped`, a mailbox holding its capacity answers
`full`). A locked step in this pin — `x64.lock add` on an x64 lane, an atomic add on an arm64
lane — is the per-message cost this case exists to keep out.

**A SEND TO A PARKED RECEIVER COPIES THE MESSAGE INTO ITS INBOX, AS GO's `sendDirect` COPIES INTO THE
RECEIVER'S ELEMENT.** A receiver parks only on an empty, open mailbox and holds the mailbox lock while it
does, so a mailbox whose parked slot is non-zero under the lock has an empty ring. The send then skips the
ring: it copies `bytes` of the staged message into the mailbox's inbox, the one slot the receiver reads each
message from, which lives in the mailbox's own region (a green thread's stack moves while the thread is
parked, so no address inside it is ever held), marks the receiver's park-argument word, which the
receiver's park commit emptied and nothing else writes while it is parked, clears the mailbox's parked slot
and leaves the lock. The receiver returns the inbox address from `__mbox_recv` without taking the lock
again. A close hands nothing: it leaves the word empty, and the receiver re-enters the lock to find the ring
empty and closed. A send that finds the parked slot empty appends to the ring, and the receiver's later pop
copies the head slot into the inbox behind any already queued, so the order is exact. A send that finds as
many messages queued as the mailbox's capacity (1024 unless the spawn names another) queues nothing and
answers `full`; a send to a closed mailbox likewise answers `stopped`, and in both the message is left in
the sender's staging buffer. The append road cuts the ring, 16 slots of the concrete service's request union
(or the capacity, when that is smaller), at the first message it has to queue, and doubles it when it is
full and still below the capacity: it copies the queued messages into the new ring in order, starting from the
head, stores the new ring and frees the old one. The ring is runtime scaffolding like a green thread's
stack, so it is cut with `__slab_alloc_scaffold` and freed with `__slab_free_scaffold`, which step none of
the allocator's traffic columns: whether a message queues depends on whether its receiver was parked, and
a timing-dependent allocation must not reach the counts.

**A SEND TO A PARKED RECEIVER READIES IT WITHOUT `__sched_lock`, AS GO's `goready` DOES.** Once the mailbox
lock is left, the send holds the service it took from the mailbox's parked slot, and readies it on one of
two roads:

- **The lock-free road.** The send claims the service's strand with a compare-and-swap of its strand
  holder from free to held. A free holder means its resume slot is 0 and no member of the strand runs, so
  the winner is the strand's one publisher and needs no lock; a member a readier pushed onto the strand
  queue while the holder was free is run by the turn this publish starts, after the resume slot. It stores the
  service's status `ready`, stores the service into the strand's resume slot (which the strand's next turn
  takes before anything else, so the owner still runs first), steps the strand's reference count, puts
  the owner's token on its processor's run queue with `__sched_runq_put`, and pays the wake with
  `__sched_wake_or_spawn`. Nothing on this road enters `__sched_lock`.
- **The locked fallback.** A failed claim means the strand is held: a coroutine of the service is queued
  or running. The send then calls `__gt_ready_locked`, which tries the claim once more and, losing it,
  pushes the service onto the front of its strand queue under the strand's own lock, for the machine
  holding the strand to find.

A `__sched_lock` enter between the strand claim and the run-queue put is the second lock per wake this case
exists to keep out.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

2

<!-- test: a-locked-ready-claims-the-strand-holder-with-a-cas -->
**EVERY CLAIM OF A STRAND's HOLDER IS A COMPARE-AND-SWAP, SO A LOCK-FREE CLAIMER AND A LOCKED ONE NEVER BOTH
WIN.** A strand's holder word says whether some machine owns the strand: free, or held while its owner's
token is in a run queue or a machine runs one of its members. Whoever turns it from free to held becomes the
strand's one publisher. A send to a parked service claims it with no lock held. `__gt_ready_locked`
readying an owner first tries the same lock-free claim, and on a win puts the owner in the resume slot and
publishes the token without touching the strand queue. Only when that claim loses, and for every coroutine,
does it push the thread onto the strand queue under the strand's own lock and then claim, still under that
lock. The lock does not exclude a lock-free claimer, so the claim after the push is the same
compare-and-swap.

The release takes no lock. The strand runner, finding its strand queue empty, turns the holder word from
held to free with one atomic add of -1, then re-reads the queue head with an acquire load, and claims the
strand back if a member arrived. A readier writes the head and then tries the claim; the releaser writes the
holder and then reads the head. That pair of write-then-read sides is a Dekker handshake, so at least one
side sees the other's write: the member is either found by the releaser's re-check or claimed by its
readier, and never left on a free strand. No claim can win against a held word, so only the holder
releases.

What this pin shows is `__gt_ready_locked`'s claim roads. The owner's arm runs one atomic compare-and-swap of
the holder word from free to held before any lock: its success stores the resume slot and publishes the
token, and its failure enters the strand lock and pushes the owner onto the front of the strand queue. The
coroutine's arm enters the strand lock and appends. Both queue roads then run the same compare-and-swap
under the lock, whose success publishes the token and whose failure answers no wake debt. A plain load of
the holder followed by a plain store of held is the window in which a lock-free claimer wins too, and two
machines run one strand.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

2
```

<!-- test: a-mailbox-receive-takes-the-mailboxs-own-lock -->
**A RECEIVE SERIALISES ONLY WITH ITS OWN MAILBOX.** A mailbox's ring, its head and count, its closed flag and
its parked receiver are guarded by a lock the mailbox carries in its own region, not by `__sched_lock`, so
two services' traffic never meets on a lock and a service's traffic never meets the scheduler's ready, park
and run-queue work. `__mbox_recv` takes that lock around its count read and its pop on the `recvtry` road,
and its `closed` read on the empty road is inside the same hold as the count read, so "empty and closed" is
one instant. The pop copies the head slot into the mailbox's inbox and answers the inbox's address, and a
ring that has grown past its first slots (16, or the capacity when that is smaller) is replaced by a fresh
ring of that size once the pop empties it. It answers 0 only on a closed, empty mailbox, which is the one
instant the service loop exits on, so no message is ever left queued behind the exit.

What this pin shows is the lock each road enters and leaves: the lock word the enter and leave operate on
is the mailbox's own lock field, computed from the `mbox` argument, and no load of `__sched_lock`
appears anywhere in the body. The empty and open road keeps the lock: it stores the running green
thread into the mailbox's `parkedGt` word and calls `__gt_park` with the lock still held, as Go's
`chanrecv` parks with `c.lock` held and `chanparkcommit` releases it. Only the drained road, which returns 0,
leaves before it returns. The hold crosses the switch to the machine's scheduler context, which releases it
on the same OS thread before any other green thread runs there (`__gt_run_strand`'s mailbox commit, pinned
by `a-strand-turn-takes-only-its-own-strands-lock`), so the lock, recursive on its owner thread, is never entered by a second
green thread and nothing can append or close between the empty read and the registration. When the
receiver resumes it reads the park-argument word: a send marked it after copying the message into the inbox,
and `__mbox_recv` returns the inbox's address without entering the lock; a close left the word empty, and
the road re-enters `recvtry`.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: a-service-message-is-copied-into-its-mailbox-with-no-allocation -->
**A MESSAGE IS NEVER A HEAP RECORD: IT IS COPIED FROM THE SENDER'S STAGING BUFFER INTO THE MAILBOX'S OWN
STORAGE, AS GO COPIES A CHANNEL ELEMENT INTO `hchan`'s BUFFER.** The send fills a buffer its green thread
owns (`__mbox_staging`, cut once from the scheduler's arena at the thread's first send and kept with its
record) with plain stores: the tag, each argument and the reply cell, in that order, and no call
stands between the last store and `__mbox_send`. `__mbox_send(mbox, msg, bytes)`, where `bytes` is the size
of the sender's request union as the parser knows it (24 here, a constant `main` passes), then copies `bytes` of it
under the mailbox lock, into the parked receiver's inbox when one is parked (Go's `sendDirect`), and
otherwise into the ring's tail slot, cutting the ring on the first message that has to be queued and
doubling it, with a copy, when it is full and below the mailbox's capacity, and answers a status:
delivered, `full` or `stopped`. `__mbox_recv(mbox)` copies the head slot into the mailbox's
one-slot inbox, shrinks a ring that has grown past its first 16 slots back to 16 once the queue is empty,
and answers the inbox address, so the loop reads the tag and each argument from that address. A payload is
moved into the staging buffer, and each copy after that moves plain words with no reference-count step.

What these pins show is the absence. `main` allocates the service's state and its handle box and nothing for
the message: its only `__mm_alloc` calls are those two. `Counter.__loop` has no `__mm_decref` of a request
shell, its only one being the state's drop on the way out, and neither has a `__mm_free`. The stores into the
staging buffer are the message, and `__mbox_staging` is the call before them, never between them and the
send. The loop has no drain after it: `__mbox_recv` answers 0 only on a closed, empty mailbox, so nothing
is left to drop when the loop exits, and its dispatch default calls `__mbox_unknown_tag`, which aborts.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: a-windows-host-lock-spins-before-it-sleeps -->
<!-- unsupported-targets: x64-linux, arm64-macos, arm64-linux -->
**ON WINDOWS, A RUNTIME LOCK SPINS BEFORE IT SLEEPS, AND SLEEPS ON ITS MACHINE's OWN EVENT, AS GO's
`lock2` DOES.** A runtime lock is a zero-initialised word, not an OS object: a zero word is a free lock, so
no lock is allocated or initialised before its first enter. A contended enter spins for a bounded count,
retrying the acquire, because a hold lasts a few instructions and a sleep and a wake cost more than it.
Only then does it record its machine as a waiter in the lock word and sleep on that machine's own event
with `WaitForSingleObject` (Go's `semasleep`); a leave that finds a waiter recorded wakes it with `SetEvent`
(Go's `semawakeup`). The event belongs to the machine and is created the first time that machine sleeps on
a lock (Go's `semacreate`), so a machine that never contends creates none.

`__sched_init_procs` is the witness because it is the first body every scheduled program runs, and it
sets up the scheduler's tables before any lock is entered: `__sched_lock`, `__gt_gfree_lock`,
`__gt_allg_lock` and `__maxon_registry_lock` among them. What this pin shows is that it calls no import for
a lock and cuts no region for one: an `InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount` call here is an OS object per
lock, and an `EnterCriticalSection` call on its uncontended enter an import call per lock round trip. The
`CreateEventA` it calls is the machine's park event, which the scheduler parks an idle machine on. The other
lanes have no CRITICAL_SECTION to rule out, so the case has no subject there.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
__sched_init_procs
```

<!-- test: a-reply-cell-writes-only-its-own-words -->
**A REPLY CELL ZEROES WHAT IT USES, AND A RECYCLED RECORD IS NOT ZEROED WHOLE.** Every awaited service
message mints a reply cell, a green-thread record that never runs: no stack, no entry, never queued. A cell
reads and writes a handful of the record's words, so filling all `GtStructSize` bytes of a recycled record
on every message is a cost the message pays for words nothing reads. `__gt_free_get` therefore hands its
taker the record as the free list held it, and each taker writes what it needs: a green-thread or `async`
spawn clears the whole record itself, and `__gt_cell_alloc` stores the cell's own words.

The record still comes from the green-thread free list, never from a separate pool, because a stale
`awaitAny` or `isComplete` read of a recycled record relies on every record in that list having the same
shape.

What this pin shows: `__gt_free_get`'s `gfgrecycle` road returns the popped record with no `memFill` over
it, and `__gt_cell_alloc` stores every word a cell is read through before it returns the cell. A
whole-record fill in either body is the per-message cost this case exists to keep out.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

__gt_cell_alloc
__gt_free_get

<!-- test: a-wake-with-no-idle-processor-takes-no-lock -->
**A PUBLISH THAT HAS NO IDLE PROCESSOR TO WAKE TAKES NO LOCK — Go's `wakep` early-out.** Every green-thread
publish ends in `__sched_wake_or_spawn`, which decides whether another machine must be started for the work
just published. A machine can only be started on an idle processor, so when `__sched_npidle` reads 0 there
is nothing to do, and the body returns after one unlocked load, before it reserves a spinner and before
`__sched_startm` takes `__sched_lock` to look for a processor it would not find. At one processor that is
every publish of the program's life.

What this pin shows is the order: the `__sched_npidle` load and its test come before the spinner
reservation's compare-and-swap and before any call that takes `__sched_lock`.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
__sched_wake_or_spawn
```

<!-- test: a-strand-turn-takes-only-its-own-strands-lock -->
**A STRAND TURN TAKES NO LOCK BUT ITS STRAND's OWN, AND THAT ONE ONLY TO POP OR PLACE A MEMBER ON THE
STRAND QUEUE.** The strand runner's consume door, `__gt_strand_next`, pops what the strand runs next, or
gives the strand up when nothing in it is runnable. The words it reads and writes belong to one strand: the
strand queue, the resume slot and the holder word, so one processor's turn never meets another's on
`__sched_lock`. Only the holder reads the resume slot. The strand queue is guarded by the strand's own lock,
which the turn takes only when an acquire load of the queue head finds a member to pop. The release takes
no lock on any strand: an atomic add turns the holder word free, an acquire re-read of the queue head
follows it, and a member pushed in between is claimed back by compare-and-swap. A strand with no
coroutines has an empty strand queue, and its one member comes back through the resume slot, so its turn
takes no lock at all. That is every service's turn, and `main`'s in a program without `async`.

A park other than a mailbox park is registered on the store the member waits on, under that store's own
lock, before the pop. The registration and the pop are therefore never two holds of one lock. A mailbox park
arrives already registered: the receiver stored itself as the mailbox's `parkedGt` while it held the mailbox
lock, so the runner only commits the park.

A yielder goes behind its siblings on its strand queue, under the strand lock. When it has no sibling, its
strand's token goes to the global run queue, and only that enqueue takes `__sched_lock`, as Go's
`goschedImpl` takes `sched.lock` only around `globrunqput`. A preempted member's token takes the same global
road.

What this pin shows is the runner's park road: `__gt_run_strand` from the switch back to the next member,
with `__gt_register_park` and `__gt_strand_next` beside it. `__gt_strand_next` enters no `__sched_lock` on
its `snfirst`, `snpop`, `snresume`, `sngot` or `snrelease` roads. It enters the strand's lock only on
`sndequeue`, the road where the acquire load of the queue head found a member. `snrelease` enters no lock at
all: it adds -1 to the holder word atomically, re-reads the queue head with an acquire load, and only when
that finds a member does `snrecheck` claim the strand back by compare-and-swap. Its cold hand-off roads give a locked owner's strand to that owner's machine (the
`tsh`, `hp`, `pidleput` and `munlink` blocks). They keep `__sched_lock` only around the idle-processor list,
the idle-machine list and the global queue, which are still the scheduler's words. For a mailbox
park, `__gt_run_strand` stores the member's `waiting` status and leaves the mailbox lock the receive carried
across the switch. It does so on the scheduler context, before `__gt_strand_next` runs, as Go's `park_m`
calls `chanparkcommit` before it schedules. The call to `__gt_strand_next` then passes 0 as the parked
member. `__gt_register_park` dispatches on the other kinds only, because a park made under the held mailbox
lock leaves nothing to re-check or undo. In `__gt_run_strand`'s yield arm, `strandplace` enters the strand
lock around the strand queue's head load and its append. `__sched_lock` appears only on the
`strandbehindeveryone` road, around `__gt_enqueue`. A `__sched_lock` enter on a coroutine-free strand's turn
puts every message a service receives on the lock every processor's scheduling takes.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

<!-- test: a-spawn-readies-its-green-thread-with-no-scheduler-lock -->
**A SPAWN PUBLISHES ITS NEW GREEN THREAD WITHOUT `__sched_lock`, AS GO's `newproc` DOES.** Go readies a new
goroutine with a `casgstatus` and a put on its own processor's run queue, and takes `sched.lock` for neither.
A newly spawned green thread heads a strand of its own that no machine holds and that has no coroutines, so
its ready needs no lock either. Nor does it need an atomic: no other machine can reach the record until its
token is published, so nothing can race a write to it. Its status is already `ready`, the zero the spawn's
fill leaves. Its strand's holder word is stored held and its strand references stored two (the owner's own
execution and the strand hold), with plain stores. It goes into the strand's resume slot rather than onto a
strand queue, and its token goes to this processor's ring, whose publish is the release that makes those
stores visible to the machine that pops it. A send to a parked service whose strand is free takes the same
resume-slot road (`emitGtReadyParkedService`), but that record is already shared, so its claim is a
compare-and-swap. A coroutine's ready takes the other road through the same door: it joins its owner's
strand queue under that strand's own lock.

What this pin shows is `__gt_ready`'s green-thread road. It stores the holder word, the strand references
and the resume slot with plain stores, publishes the token to the ring, then calls `__sched_wake_or_spawn`,
with no `__sched_lock` enter or leave anywhere on it. The coroutine road takes the strand lock of the coroutine's
owner around the strand-queue append. A `__sched_lock` enter in this body is a serialisation every spawn
of the program's life would pay. It would also contend with every processor's scheduling, which is the
lock's remaining work.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```RequiredRuntime
__gt_ready
```

<!-- test: a-completion-hands-its-awaiter-over-under-the-promises-own-lock -->
**A COMPLETION MEETS ITS AWAITER UNDER THE PROMISE's OWN LOCK, AS GO's `hchan.lock` DOES, NOT UNDER
`__sched_lock`.** A promise's awaiter word, in the record of the coroutine or reply cell it names, has two
writers. The registrant stores itself there when it parks on the promise. The completer, in
`__gt_runner_done`, takes it and readies it. They meet under a lock word in that same record, so a
completion contends only with the one waiter of its one promise, and two replies completing on two
processors share no lock. A select's tagged awaiter is claimed by a compare-and-swap of the selector's
`selectDone` word from pending to readied. When several of its slots complete at once, each holding only its
own promise's lock, exactly one of them readies the selector. The ready of the claimed awaiter is its
strand's business, after the promise's lock is left: an awaiter that owns its strand claims the free strand
with no lock, an owner whose strand the completing machine itself holds is readied through the resume slot
with no lock (`runnerreadyheld`), and a coroutine, or an owner whose strand another machine holds, joins the
strand queue under the strand's own lock.

What this pin shows is `__gt_runner_done`'s `runnerawaiter` road. The promise's lock is entered before the
awaiter word is loaded and left after the word is cleared. The select road claims `selectDone` with an
atomic compare-and-swap rather than a load and a store. Neither road enters or leaves `__sched_lock`. The
seed-window close, `runnerseedwindow`, runs `__gt_seed_adapt` when the processor's own sample count reaches
a multiple of the window, and a compare-and-swap on the seed guard chooses the one closer. The one `__sched_lock` hold in the body is
`runnermaindone`'s: the process phase moves to draining under the lock that `__sched_checkdead` and the exit
drain read it under, as Go's `sched.lock` covers its own shutdown state. The awaiter road reaches
`__sched_lock` only through the wake debt it may pay: `runnerwake` calls `__sched_wake_or_spawn`, which
takes it to start an idle machine on an idle processor, as Go's `wakep` takes `sched.lock` in `startm`, and
skips it when no processor is idle.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

<!-- test: a-record-refill-takes-the-free-lists-own-lock -->
**A GREEN-THREAD RECORD COMES FROM THE FREE LIST UNDER THE FREE LIST's OWN LOCK, AS GO's `gfget` TAKES
`sched.gFree.lock`.** Every spawn and every awaited reply takes a record. A processor serves most of them
from its local free list with no lock. When that list is empty, `__gt_free_get` moves a batch from the
global free list, and when the global list is empty too it carves a fresh record. The global list and the
carve are the free list's words, so they are guarded by a lock of their own. The new record's append to the
`allg` roster takes the roster's lock, as Go's `allgadd` takes `allglock`. A thread that holds no processor
takes from the global list under the same free-list lock.

**THE STACKS ON THE GLOBAL LIST ARE FREED WHEN THE SEED WINDOW CLOSES, AS GO's `markrootFreeGStacks` FREES
`sched.gFree.stack` IN THE CYCLE THAT RECOMPUTES `startingStackSize`.** A record a processor sheds keeps its
stack and goes on the list of records with one, and a processor's own list keeps fewer than `GtFreeLocalHigh`
of them, Go's own bound. `__gt_runner_done`, at the finish that closes a window of `GtSeedWindowSamples`
finishes on a processor, calls `__gt_seed_adapt` and then walks the global list in its own body, because
a function between the two would put one more frame in the unguarded chain that ends in the stack pool's
lock and overflow the guard margin on x64-linux. It takes the free-list lock only to detach the whole
list of records with a stack (`__gt_gfree_head`), frees each record's stack with the lock released
(`gfswalkbody`, through `stackdrop`), and takes the lock again to put the whole chain on the list of records
without one (`__gt_gfree_nostack_head`, `gfsrelist`), in the order it had. The records are on no list while
their stacks are freed, so no taker can reach one. Every record shed before a window's last close has lost its
stack by that close, and at most the sheds after the last close of a burst keep theirs: a shutdown that
reclaims hundreds of records, as `thread-ring` does, runs through several closes, since each record's finish
is one of the window's samples.

What this pin shows is `__gt_free_get`'s three locked roads: the `gfgrefill` batch move, the `gfgnoproc`
global take and the `gfgcarve` carve. Each enters and leaves the free-list lock, and the carve's roster
append takes the `allg` lock inside it. The global take prefers a record that carries a stack when the
caller wants one, as Go's `gfget` prefers `sched.gFree.stack`, and a record without one when the caller
wants none, as a reply cell does (`gfgglobalcell` against `gfgglobalspawn`). A record that carries a stack
of any other size than the one the caller wants has the stack freed on `stackkeepdrop`, after the lock is
left, and a caller that wants a stack and is handed a record with none gets one on `gfgneedstack`, also
after the lock is left. No road enters `__sched_lock`. A `__sched_lock` enter on the refill road would put every processor's record refill on the lock every processor's scheduling takes.

**A CARVED RECORD's OWN LOCK NEEDS NO INIT, BECAUSE A ZERO WORD IS A FREE LOCK, AS GO's `mutex` IS.** The record's lock is a word in
the record, and the scheduler's arena hands out pages that arrive zeroed, so a carved record's lock is free
the moment the record is carved. The `gfgcarve` road calls `__sched_arena_carve` and then appends to the
roster, with no lock-init call between them. An init there is an OS call on every fresh record, paid by
every spawn that finds both free lists empty.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: a-runtime-lock-enter-is-an-atomic-on-its-word-with-no-call -->
**A RUNTIME LOCK IS ONE WORD, AND ITS UNCONTENDED ENTER AND LEAVE ARE BYTE EXCHANGES ON THAT WORD WITH NO CALL
AND NO LOOP, AS GO's `lock2` AND `unlock2` ARE.** A runtime lock — the scheduler's, the free list's, the roster's, a
mailbox's, a record's — is held for a few instructions and taken on every message, spawn and wake, so its
uncontended round trip is a cost all of them pay. The lock is a word that reads zero when free, whose low byte holds the held bit and a hint
that sleepers are stacked, and whose spinner bit, sleeper-stack lock and sleeper pointer sit above that
byte. The enter is the machine's lock-depth step and one exchange of the low byte for the held bit, which
took the lock when it displaced zero; the leave is one exchange of the low byte for zero, then the depth
step back. Neither is a compare-and-swap loop, and neither calls anything: no import, no chunk, no runtime
function. The OS is reached only when the exchange displaced something else: an enter whose exchange
displaced a nonzero byte calls the slow body, which spins for a bounded count and sleeps on its machine's own
semaphore, and a leave whose exchange displaced a byte other than the bare held bit calls its slow body,
which wakes a sleeper if the hint was set. A spinner recorded above the low byte does not send a leave out of
line, because the exchange does not touch it.

**THE SCHEDULER'S LOCK IS RECURSIVE ON AN OWNER TOKEN, WHICH GO's IS NOT.** A recursive lock carries an
owner slot and a depth slot beside its word, and its enter stores the calling OS thread's own block there
as the owner token, so a machine that already holds the lock finds its own token and steps the hold's
depth instead of waiting. The scheduler re-enters `__sched_lock` on its timer and netpoll paths, which run
under a hold of it; Go's timers and netpoll are per processor and take no nested scheduler lock.

`__mbox_close` is the witness because its work is one lock round trip: it enters its mailbox's lock, stores
the closed flag, and leaves on each of its two roads. What this pin shows is that round trip. A call between
the depth step up and the store of the closed flag, or between a road's last store and its depth step down
— an `iatCall` on x64-windows, an `importCall` on arm64-macos, a `callDirect` or `bl` to a lock body on the
Linux lanes — is the per-lock cost this case exists to keep out. A call into the lock's contended path
appears only behind the compare of the displaced byte.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

2
```

<!-- test: a-mailbox-lock-is-a-zero-word-with-no-init-and-no-destroy -->
**A MAILBOX's LOCK NEEDS NO INIT AND NO DESTROY, BECAUSE A ZERO WORD IS A FREE LOCK, AS GO's `hchan.lock`
IS.** `__svc_spawn` takes the mailbox's region from `__slab_alloc`, which zeroes it, so the mailbox's lock
is free the moment the region exists, and the spawn stores only the words a zero would be wrong for. When
the last reference goes, the free roads of `__mbox_handle_drop_box` and `__mbox_service_exit` hand the
region to `__slab_free`, and the message ring when a message was ever queued to `__slab_free_scaffold`, the
uncounted door the ring was cut through, and to nothing else: a free lock word holds no OS object to release.

What this pin shows is the three bodies' calls. `__svc_spawn` calls `__slab_alloc`, `__gt_spawn_green` and
`__gt_ready`, and nothing between the region's arrival and its first store; each free road calls
`__slab_free` and `__slab_free_scaffold` alone. An OS call at either place — `InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount` or
`DeleteCriticalSection` on x64-windows, a pthread mutex init or destroy on arm64-macos, a lock-init body on
the Linux lanes — is a cost every service pays at its spawn and its teardown.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

__svc_spawn
__mbox_handle_drop_box
__mbox_service_exit

<!-- test: a-spawn-from-a-record-with-a-stack-allocates-none -->
**A SPAWN FROM A RECORD THAT STILL CARRIES A FITTING STACK ALLOCATES NO STACK, AS GO's `gfget` HANDS BACK A
`g` WITH ITS STACK STILL ATTACHED.** A finished green thread's record keeps its stack when the stack is the
current seed size, exactly as `gfput` keeps a `g`'s stack when it equals `startingStackSize`; a stack of any
other size, grown or shrunk, goes back to the stack pool as the thread's runner finishes with it
(`__gt_runner_done`), before the record is put on a free list.
`__gt_free_get` is handed the seed size the spawn wants and drops the stack of a record that carries another
size, so what it returns either carries a stack of the seed size or none. A recycled record with none, and a
freshly carved record, are given a stack by `__gt_free_get` itself, as `gfget` and `malg` attach one before
`newproc1` goes on, so a carved record's first touch is `__gt_free_get`'s write of its stack words and not a
read of its fresh arena page that the write then faults a second time.

What this pin shows is `__gt_spawn`. The seed word is loaded once, before the record is taken, and is passed
to `__gt_free_get`. The record's two stack words are not zeroed: the first `memFill` ends at the stack base
and the second starts after the stack size, and the stack base is loaded only after them, to lay the first
frame. `__gt_spawn` calls no `__gt_stack_alloc` and has no refused-seed abort; both are
`__gt_free_get`'s (`gfgneedstack`). A fill over the two words would zero the stack `__gt_free_get` attached,
and the first frame would be laid one seed size above address 0.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

function twice(n Integer) returns Integer
	Scheduler.yield()

	return n * 2
end 'twice'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let p = async twice(4)
	let a = await p

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: a-stack-takes-the-pool-lock-only-to-refill-or-release -->
**A STACK COMES FROM A PER-PROCESSOR CACHE AND GOES BACK TO IT, AS GO's `stackalloc` AND `stackfree` USE
`mcache.stackcache`, AND THE POOL's LOCK IS TAKEN ONLY TO MOVE A HALF-BATCH.** Each processor holds, for
each small size class (2 KiB to 16 KiB, the classes no larger than half of `GtStackCacheCapacityBytes`; Go's
four orders), a list of free stacks and the bytes on it. The processor's machine is the only one that
touches them, so an allocation that finds a cached stack pops it, and a free pushes it, with no lock and no
atomic. An empty cache refills from the pool until it holds half of `GtStackCacheCapacityBytes`, and a free
that fills the cache to the capacity releases back to the pool until it holds half, both under the pool's one
lock, as `stackcacherefill` and `stackcacherelease` move half of `_StackCacheSize` under `stackpool`'s lock.
A thread with no machine, or a machine with no processor, has no cache and takes the pool lock for its one
stack, and so does a stack of a larger class, as Go's `stackalloc` takes the lock for a large stack. A size
above the pool's largest class is mapped and unmapped directly. The link of a stack on a list is written into
the stack's own first word, as Go's `stackfree` writes it.

What this pin shows is the two bodies. In `__gt_stack_alloc` the pool lock is entered on `stkrefill`, the
road an empty cache takes, and on `stkpoolonly`, the road of a larger class or of no processor, and nowhere
else: `stkcached` pops a cached stack through `stkpopcached` with no lock. In `__gt_stack_free` the lock is
entered on `stkrelease` and `stkpoolonly` alone, and `stkcached` pushes the stack, compares the cache's bytes
against the capacity, and returns on `stkkept` with no lock when they are below it. A lock enter on the cached
road would put every stack a processor allocates on one lock every processor takes.

**A REFILL HANDS ITS STACKS OUT IN THE ORDER THE POOL CARVED THEM, ASCENDING, AS GO's DOUBLE REVERSAL DOES.**
`stackpoolalloc` lists a span's stacks last-carved first and `stackcacherefill` pushes each at the cache's
head, so the two reversals cancel and the cache pops lowest first. The refill here carves ascending, so it
appends each stack at the list's tail instead of pushing it at the head: the loop carries the last stack
taken (`stkrefilltop`'s block argument, which starts as the cache entry, whose head word sits where a stack's
link does), and `stkrefillgot` stores the new stack through it. A push at the head would pop the highest
address of the batch first.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```

<!-- test: a-completion-steps-no-global-counter-for-the-seed-or-the-trace -->
**A COMPLETION SAMPLES ITS STACK INTO ITS OWN PROCESSOR'S WORDS, AND A SPAWN NUMBERS A THREAD ONLY WHEN
SOMETHING READS THE NUMBER.** The adaptive seed is Go's `startingStackSize`, which `gcComputeStartingStackSize`
recomputes from per-processor `scannedStackSize` and `scannedStacks` that each processor adds to with plain
instructions. Here `__gt_runner_done` adds the finished stack's size and one to the current processor's two
words, and the add that makes the processor's count a multiple of the window closes the window with
`__gt_seed_adapt`. The close sums every processor's words under its own claim, so a completion makes no
`lock add` and no `lock xadd` on a word every processor shares. A thread with no processor takes no sample.
The trace id, the number an async trace line or a DebugStream event names a thread by, is minted only in a
build that has one of the two. Without them `__gt_spawn` stores no id and touches no counter for it. The live
count stays an atomic step per spawn, because the exit drain waits on it.

What this pin shows is `__gt_runner_done`'s `runnersampled` road and `__gt_spawn`'s tail. `runnersampled`
loads the current processor, and `runnercountsample` adds to its sum and count with plain loads and stores,
masks the count with the window and calls `__gt_seed_adapt` from `runnerseedwindow` only on a multiple.
`__gt_seed_adapt` claims `__gt_seed_guard` by compare-and-swap, sums the processors' words in `seedsumbody`,
and publishes a new seed only when the sums hold at least a window of samples more than the last close saw.
No atomic step on the completion road names a shared word. `__gt_spawn` steps `__gt_live_count` atomically
and contains no block of the `traceid` family and no reference to `__gt_trace_counter`. A shared atomic on the
completion road is a locked cache line every processor's completions fight over.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

function twice(n Integer) returns Integer
	Scheduler.yield()

	return n * 2
end 'twice'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let p = async twice(4)
	let a = await p

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

8
```

<!-- test: a-record-carve-takes-the-free-list-lock-once -->
**A CARVE TAKES THE FREE LIST's LOCK ONCE, AND THE ROSTER's LOCK ONCE, AS GO's `malg` PAIRS `allgadd` WITH ONE
HOLD OF THE LOCK THAT COVERS THE ALLOCATION.** The arena's cursor and limit belong to `__gt_gfree_lock`. A
record's carve and a machine's carve (`emitSchedAllocM`, under `__sched_lock`) each hold it around the
`__sched_arena_carve` call, and the carve itself takes nothing. A record's carve is made inside the hold that
already consulted every free list, so it is one hold, and the new record's append to the `allg` roster
takes the roster's lock inside it, as Go's `allgadd` takes `allglock`.

What this pin shows is `__gt_free_get`'s `gfgcarve` road and the arena carve beside it. `gfgcarve` calls
`__sched_arena_carve`, steps the carved count, appends to the roster, and leaves the free-list lock once,
which closes the one hold that `gfgrefill` or `gfgnoproc` opened. `__sched_arena_carve` has no lock enter and
no lock leave. A second enter of the free-list lock around the carve is a recursive-lock round trip on every
fresh record.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```

<!-- test: a-completion-readies-its-strands-owner-with-no-record-lock -->
**A COROUTINE'S COMPLETION READIES ITS OWN STRAND'S OWNER THROUGH THE RESUME SLOT, WITH NO LOCK, BECAUSE THE
MACHINE THAT COMPLETED IT HOLDS THE STRAND.** `main` awaits a coroutine of its own strand. The strand runner
that switched into the coroutine is the strand's holder, so when the coroutine completes, the owner it
readies cannot be claimed by anyone else: the holder word reads held, and the only machine that may write the
strand's resume slot is the holder. The runner hands `__gt_runner_done` the strand it holds. When the
awaiter is that strand's owner, the completion compares the status word from `waiting` to `ready` and stores
the owner into `GtOffStrandResume`, which `__gt_strand_next` takes before the strand queue. Every other
awaiter, a coroutine or an owner whose strand another machine holds, is readied by `__gt_ready_locked`, which
claims a free strand with no lock and otherwise joins the strand queue under the strand's own lock. The
callers that are not a strand runner pass no strand.

What this pin shows is `__gt_runner_done`'s `runnerplainawaiter` road, which leaves the promise's lock and
compares the awaiter against the strand it was handed. `runnerreadyheld` has one atomic compare-and-swap, one
store and no lock enter. `runnerreadyelsewhere` is the only block that calls `__gt_ready_locked`. A strand
lock enter on the held road is a recursive-lock round trip and a queue push per `await` of a coroutine, paid
by every program that awaits one.

```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

function twice(n Integer) returns Integer
	Scheduler.yield()

	return n * 2
end 'twice'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let p = async twice(4)
	let a = await p

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
8
```

<!-- test: a-windows-blocking-import-carries-the-last-error-across-a-lost-processor -->
<!-- unsupported-targets: x64-linux, arm64-macos, arm64-linux -->
**ON WINDOWS, A BLOCKING IMPORT'S LAST ERROR SURVIVES THE SCHEDULER'S SLOW EXIT, AS GO's SYSCALL PATH CAPTURES IT
BEFORE `exitsyscall`.** A caller reads the error of a failed import with a separate `GetLastError` call
right after the import returns. When `__sysmon` took the machine's processor during the import, the shim's
exit calls `__sched_syscall_regain`, whose lock road may create the machine's first lock event
(`CreateEventA`) and so rewrite the thread's `LastErrorValue`. The slow exit therefore reads the TEB's
`LastErrorValue` (`gs:[0x68]`) into a frame slot beside the saved result before the call, and writes it back
after the call.

`mrt_write_stream` is the witness because its raw-byte road calls `WriteFile`, a `blocking` import, through
the shim, so the shim's exit is emitted inside this one chunk. What the bytes show is a `mov ecx, gs:[0x68]`
and a store to `[rsp + 0x28]` ahead of the `call`, and a load from `[rsp + 0x28]` and a `mov gs:[0x68], ecx`
after it, around the `rax` result's own `[rsp + 0x20]` store and reload. A slow exit with neither is the one
that lets a failed `FindNextFileW`'s `ERROR_NO_MORE_FILES` read as 0. The posix lanes keep their error in a
word only the runtime's own failure arms write, which the regain road never reaches, so the case has no
subject there.
```maxon
typealias Integer = int(i64.min to i64.max)

type Counter
	var calls as Integer

	static function create() returns Self
		return Self{calls: 0}
	end 'create'

	export function next(n Integer) returns Integer
		self.calls = self.calls + 1

		return n + 1
	end 'next'
end 'Counter'

function main() returns ExitCode
	let c = spawn Counter.create()
	let a = try await c.next(1) otherwise 0

	print("done\n")

	return a as ExitCode
end 'main'
```
```exitcode
2
```
```stdout
done
```
```RequiredRuntime
mrt_write_stream
```
